claims.evidence: Inferred from bite-back experiment data in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4C

claims.claim: Saglin knockout mutants bear no fitness cost at least in laboratory conditions.
claims.source: Because Saglin knockout mutants bear no fitness cost at least in laboratory conditions, GD-refractory Saglin alleles generated by failed homing events are certain to accumulate over time
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Klug et al., 2023

claims.claim: A Lp suppression GD was constructed with an array of 4 gRNAs targeting Lp but not Lp::Sc2A10, expressed under control of a single U6 promoter.
claims.source: We constructed a DsRedNLS-marked Lp suppression GD (Figure 3A and annotated sequence in Supplementary file 1C), in which an array of 4 gRNAs separated by tRNAs (Xie et al., 2015; Port and Bullock, 2016), targeting Lp but not Lp::Sc2A10, were expressed under control of a single U6 promoter.
claims.evidence: Described as experimental design in Results and illustrated in Figure 3A

claims.claim: Cas9 was placed under the control of zpg regulatory elements in the Lp suppression GD.
claims.source: Cas9 was placed under the control of zpg regulatory elements, currently considered best for use in suppression GDs due to tighter restriction of Cas9 activity to the germ line (Kyrou et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Described as experimental design in Results and supported by citations

claims.claim: Most knock-in events unexpectedly arose from compound recombinations between the cleaved WT chromosome and both the repair template plasmid and the intact Lp::Sc2A10 sister chromosome.
claims.source: Puzzlingly however, the majority of knock-in larvae contained a compound Lp locus harboring the DsRedNLS-marked GD cassette strictly linked to the GFP-marked Lp::Sc2A10 transgene. Sequencing PCR products spanning parts of this insertion confirmed that, instead of the expected insertion of the Lp-GD cassette, a complex chromosomal rearrangement (Figure 3B) had repaired the Cas9-cleaved wild-type chromosome by incorporating the entire injected plasmid, and by recombining with the intact sister chromosome bearing the Lp::Sc2A10 transgene.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data and genetic linkage analysis described in Results and illustrated in Figure 3B

claims.claim: The GFP-RFP Lp allele was homozygous viable.
claims.source: The resulting unintended transgenic modification at the Lp locus harbored all the components of a classical payload-bearing GD that we hereinafter refer to as GFP-RFP. Similarly to the Lp::Sc2A10 allele, the GFP-RFP Lp allele was homozygous viable, functional Lp protein being expressed from its Lp::Sc2A10 moiety.
claims.evidence: Based on observation of mosquito populations in the laboratory

claims.claim: The GFP-RFP allele was inherited in about 50% of male or female progenies, demonstrating little homing activity after crosses to WT.
claims.source: In spite of the presence of the zpg-Cas9 and gRNA-encoding cassettes in the GFP-RFP allele, it was inherited in about 50% of male or female progenies, demonstrating little homing activity of the GFP-RFP locus after crosses to WT, except for the appearance of rare GFP-only or RFP-only progeny larvae, raising concern about the efficiency of the zpg-Cas9 and/or the gRNA-expressing cassettes.
claims.evidence: Based on genetic crosses and progeny analysis described in Results

claims.claim: Providing an independent copy of vasa-Cas9 on a different chromosome rescued the homing defect and resulted in high homing rates of various segments from the GFP-RFP cassette.
claims.source: Providing an independent copy of vasa-Cas9 on a different chromosome rescued this defect and resulted in high homing rates of various segments from the GFP-RFP cassette (mostly GFP alone, more rarely DsRedNLS alone or both) (Figure 4A), indicating that at least some of the gRNAs in the tRNA-spaced array were active and that the defect was in zpg-Cas9 expression.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 4A

claims.claim: Heterozygous mosquitoes carrying one copy of Lp-GD and either GFP-RFP or Lp::Sc2A10 showed a striking developmental delay and died before adulthood.
claims.source: Most heterozygous mosquitoes carrying one copy of Lp-GD and either GFP-RFP or Lp::Sc2A10 (both of which should be refractory to homing of the GD construct) showed a striking developmental delay and died before adulthood (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by observation and photograph in Figure 4B

claims.claim: Heterozygous mosquitoes carrying Lp-GD / WT survived to adulthood but were small and short-lived.
claims.source: Heterozygous mosquitoes carrying Lp-GD / WT survived to adulthood but were small and short-lived.
claims.evidence: Based on observation of mosquito populations in the laboratory

claims.claim: WT Lp is largely haplo-insufficient in presence of a Lp loss-of-function allele.
claims.source: These observations indicate that WT Lp is largely haplo-insufficient in presence of a Lp loss-of-function allele, even more so if WT Lp is replaced by Lp::Sc2A10.
claims.evidence: Inferred from developmental delay and lethality data in Figure 4B

claims.claim: It was impossible to create a loss-of function GD in the Lp locus due to haplo-insufficiency of Lp.
claims.source: From the haplo-insufficiency of Lp we concluded that it was impossible to create a loss-of function GD in this locus, precluding an indirect same-locus GD approach.
claims.evidence: Inferred from haplo-insufficiency data

claims.claim: The zpg promoter appeared to have low activity when integrated in the Lp locus.
claims.source: In addition, the zpg promoter appeared to have low activity when integrated in the Lp locus.
claims.evidence: Inferred from low homing rates observed with zpg-Cas9 constructs

claims.claim: Saglin encodes a Plasmodium agonist.
claims.source: To host a GD promoting the spread of Lp::Sc2A10, we turned our attention to the mosquito Saglin locus, which encodes a Plasmodium agonist (Okulate et al., 2007; Ghosh et al., 2009; O'Brochta et al., 2019; Klug et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Okulate et al., 2007; Ghosh et al., 2009; O'Brochta et al., 2019; Klug et al., 2023

claims.claim: The loss of Saglin reduces parasite prevalence and loads, reduces transmission, is homozygous viable and has no obvious fitness cost at least in laboratory conditions.
claims.source: Indeed, while not leading to complete Plasmodium transmission blockage, the loss of Saglin reduces parasite prevalence and loads, reduces transmission, is homozygous viable and has no obvious fitness cost at least in laboratory conditions (Klug et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Klug et al., 2023

claims.claim: A gene drive cassette comprising Cas9 under control of the zpg promoter and an array of 7 gRNAs was inserted disruptively in the endogenous Saglin open reading frame.
claims.source: To exclude that the low zpg-Cas9 activity we previously observed at the Lp locus was due to overlooked mutations in our construct, we subcloned the zpg-Cas9 cassette from a validated GD construct (Kyrou et al., 2018) and incorporated it in a Saglin knock-in plasmid expressing Cas9, DsRedNLS, 3 gRNAs directed against Saglin and 4 gRNAs against Lp (Figure 5, and annotated sequence of this plasmid in Supplementary file 1D).
claims.evidence: Described as experimental design in Results and illustrated in Figure 5A

claims.claim: 100% of the G1 transgenics arising from injected males were females, an indication that the construct had correctly homed onto the X chromosome, where Saglin is located.
claims.source: 100% of the G1 transgenics arising from injected males were females, an indication that the construct had correctly homed onto the X chromosome, where Saglin is located.
claims.evidence: Based on genetic crosses and progeny analysis described in Results

claims.claim: All G1 transgenics had also inherited a copy of Lp::Sc2A10 (GFP positive), instead of the expected 50%.
claims.source: In addition, all G1 transgenics had also inherited a copy of Lp::Sc2A10 (GFP positive), instead of the expected 50%. This suggests that the GD construct acted on the Lp locus, causing either efficient Lp::Sc2A10 homing already in the germ line of G0 males, and/or the death of larvae that did not inherit a protected Lp copy due to the toxicity of the construct's Lp gRNAs.
claims.evidence: Based on genetic crosses and progeny analysis described in Results

claims.claim: The first Saglin GD (SagGDzpg) showed disappointingly modest homing levels at both the Saglin and Lp loci in the G2 generation.
claims.source: In spite of the efficiency of zpg-Cas9 for initial integration, this first Saglin GD (termed SagGDzpg) showed disappointingly modest homing levels at both the Saglin and Lp loci in the G2 generation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 6A

claims.claim: GFP inheritance was 57.7% (Lp::Sc2A10 locus) compared to 50% expected in the absence of homing.
claims.source: Using COPAS flow cytometry, we examined GFP and DsRed inheritance in 2327 larvae that arose from the pooled G1 females crossed to WT males. It showed 57.7% GFP inheritance (Lp::Sc2A10 locus) compared to 50% expected in the absence of homing.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 6A

claims.claim: DsRed inheritance was approximately 54.1% at the Saglin locus.
claims.source: DsRed inheritance was more difficult to assess, as the low intensity of red fluorescence did not allow accurate gating to separate red fluorescent from negative larvae on COPAS diagrams. Approximate gating completed with visual examination of a sample of 200 larvae suggested 54.1% DsRed inheritance at the Saglin locus, an even more modest inheritance bias than for GFP at the Lp locus.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 6A

claims.claim: The progeny of triple-transgenic females carrying SagGDzpg, Lp::Sc2A10 and vasa-Cas9 crossed to WT males showed markedly better homing rates (>79% GFP inheritance).
claims.source: To distinguish among these possibilities, we generated females carrying single heterozygous copies of the three unlinked transgenes SagGDzpg, Lp::Sc2A10 and a non-fluorescent (puromycin resistance-marked) vasa-Cas9. The progeny of these triple-transgenic females crossed to WT males showed markedly better homing rates (>79% GFP inheritance) (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 6B

claims.claim: vasa-Cas9 was able to significantly rescue the modest homing rate of zpg-Cas9 from SagGDzpg, resulting in an efficient split GD.
claims.source: Thus, vasa-Cas9 was able to significantly rescue the modest homing rate of zpg-Cas9 from SagGDzpg, resulting in an efficient split GD.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of homing rates in Figures 6A and 6B

claims.claim: The cloned zpg promoter sequence is sensitive to positional effects, being poorly active when inserted in Saglin or Lp in contrast to other previously reported host loci such as DSX or Nudel.
claims.source: This suggests that the cloned zpg promoter sequence is sensitive to positional effects, being poorly active when inserted in Saglin or Lp in contrast to other previously reported host loci such as DSX or Nudel (Kyrou et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Inferred from homing rate data and supported by citations

claims.claim: One mosquito population of Lp::Sc2A10 combined with SagGDzpg showed an increase in the frequency of both alleles after seven generations (G7: GFP allelic frequency = 59.2%, phenotypic expression of DsRed in >90% of larvae, n=4282 larvae).
claims.source: We maintained one mosquito population of Lp::Sc2A10 combined with SagGDzpg (initial allele frequencies: 25% and 33%, respectively) and measured genotype frequencies after seven generations. This showed an increase in the frequency of both alleles (G7: GFP allelic frequency = 59.2%, phenotypic expression of DsRed in >90% of larvae, n=4282 larvae), indicating that the modest GD strength of SagGDzpg was still able to increase the frequency of the SagGDzpg allele over time and counteract the Lp::Sc2A10 fitness cost.
claims.evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of mosquito populations over generations

claims.claim: Two versions of SagGDvasa were initially made: one carrying a complex array of seven gRNAs and another carrying six tandem U6-gRNA units.
claims.source: We initially made two versions of SagGDvasa: one carrying the complex array of seven gRNAs described above for SagGDzpg (as in Figure 5A); another carrying six tandem U6-gRNA units (Figure 5B; sequence provided in Supplementary file 1E).
claims.evidence: Described as experimental design in Results and illustrated in Figure 5

claims.claim: About 20 DsRed positive G1 females and no positive male were recovered from outcrossing G0 injected males to WT females, again an indication of proper insertion of the GD cassette onto the X chromosome.
claims.source: About 35 surviving G0 injected male mosquitoes (which were homozygous for Lp::Sc2A10 to prevent any premature damage on Lp), outcrossed to WT females, yielded about 20 DsRed positive G1 females and no positive male, again an indication of proper insertion of the GD cassette onto the X chromosome, where Saglin is located.
claims.evidence: Based on genetic crosses and progeny analysis described in Results

claims.claim: G1 females heterozygous at both SagGDvasa on the X chromosome and Lp::Sc2A10 on the second chromosome developed normally to adulthood and were fertile when crossed to wild-type males.
claims.source: These G1 females (heterozygous at both SagGDvasa on the X chromosome and Lp::Sc2A10 on the second chromosome) developed normally to adulthood and were fertile when crossed to wild-type males.
claims.evidence: Based on observation of mosquito populations in the laboratory

claims.claim: High homing rates at both loci were recorded in G2 by examining the progeny of the individual G1 females backcrossed to WT males, a large majority of progeny inheriting both a SagGDvasa copy (DsRedNLS) and a Lp::Sc2A10 copy (GFP).
claims.source: High homing rates at both loci were recorded in G2 by examining the progeny of the individual G1 females backcrossed to WT males, a large majority of progeny inheriting both a SagGDvasa copy (DsRedNLS) and a Lp::Sc2A10 copy (GFP) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by genetic crosses and progeny analysis in Table 2

claims.claim: The male cross yielded only 405 larvae, of which 391 were GFP positive (GFP inheritance: 96.5%, corresponding to a homing rate of 93%).
claims.source: The male cross yielded only 405 larvae, of which 391 were GFP positive (GFP inheritance: 96.5%, corresponding to a homing rate of 93%).
claims.evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of progeny from genetic crosses

claims.claim: The female cross yielded 5197 larvae showing 95.1% GFP inheritance and 80.7% DsRed inheritance, corresponding to homing rates of 90.2% at the Lp locus and 61.4% at the Saglin locus.
claims.source: The female cross yielded 5197 larvae showing 95.1% GFP inheritance and 80.7% DsRed inheritance, corresponding to homing rates of 90.2% at the Lp locus and 61.4% at the Saglin locus.
claims.evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of progeny from genetic crosses

claims.claim: The vasa promoter was highly active in germ cells when inserted in the Saglin locus.
claims.source: Thus, in contrast to zpg, the vasa promoter was highly active in germ cells when inserted in the Saglin locus.
claims.evidence: Inferred from high homing rates observed with vasa-Cas9 constructs

claims.claim: Saglin was undetectable in SagGDvasa mosquitoes by western blotting.
claims.source: To verify that SagGDvasa abolished Saglin expression, we dissected salivary glands from control and homozygous DsRed +mosquito females, and subjected them to western blotting using anti-Saglin antibodies. As expected, Saglin was undetectable in SagGDvasa mosquitoes (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 5C

claims.claim: In all populations, mosquitoes lacking Lp::Sc2A10 disappeared rapidly, and all young populations rapidly consisted of a majority of homozygous Lp::Sc2A10 mosquitoes.
claims.source: In all populations, mosquitoes lacking Lp::Sc2A10 disappeared rapidly, and all young populations rapidly consisted of a majority of homozygous Lp::Sc2A10 mosquitoes (Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claims.claim: DsRed-only individuals were strikingly absent from all early populations, indicative of the lethality of the SagGDvasa transgene in the absence of a protected Lp allele.
claims.source: Despite the absence of physical linkage between the two transgenes, DsRed-only individuals were strikingly absent from all early populations, indicative of the lethality of the SagGDvasa transgene in the absence of a protected Lp allele.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claims.claim: Toxicity of SagGDvasa was due to its destructive action on the Lp locus rather than to a fitness cost of its disrupted Saglin host locus.
claims.source: Importantly, toxicity of SagGDvasa was due to its destructive action on the Lp locus rather than to a fitness cost of its disrupted Saglin host locus, since individuals carrying both DsRed and GFP thrived in all populations, and consistent with the reported absence of obvious fitness cost of Saglin mutants (Klug et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Inferred from population dynamics data and supported by citation to Klug et al., 2023

claims.claim: Several populations (notably populations 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) rapidly seemed fixed for Lp::Sc2A10.
claims.source: Several populations (notably populations 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) rapidly seemed fixed for Lp::Sc2A10.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claims.claim: A trend for reversal, with Lp::Sc2A10 progressively giving way to GFP negative individuals, was observed from G14 on for population 2.
claims.source: A trend for reversal, with Lp::Sc2A10 progressively giving way to GFP negative individuals (presumably functional Lp mutants refractory to homing), was observed from G14 on for population 2, although GFP positive individuals still represented a large majority of the population (>90% from G1 on), while GFP allele frequency reached 0.98 at G8 before decreasing and oscillating between 0.71 and 0.92 after G14.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claims.claim: A substantial fraction of DsRed negative individuals (up to 30%), likely carrying GD refractory Saglin mutants, persisted in some populations.
claims.source: While the majority of mosquitoes of all populations rapidly carried at least one copy of SagGDvasa, we observed that a substantial fraction of DsRed negative individuals (up to 30%), likely carrying GD refractory Saglin mutants, persisted in some populations (Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claims.claim: DsRed negative mosquitoes represented 18 and 31% of populations 1 and 2, respectively, at the generations sampled.
claims.source: To characterize Saglin mutants, we COPAS-extracted 750 and 150 DsRed-negative larvae from a surplus of larvae from generation 4 of population 1 and generation 3 of population 2. DsRed-negative individuals represented 18 and 31% of these populations, respectively, with the Saglin gene on their X chromosome having been exposed to between one and four rounds of Cas9 activity.
claims.evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of mosquito populations

claims.claim: The majority of sequenced DsRed negative alleles still corresponded to wild-type Saglin having thus far escaped GD activity.
claims.source: While the majority of sequenced DsRed negative alleles still corresponded to wild-type Saglin having thus far escaped GD activity, a wide variety of Saglin mutations, different between the two sampled populations, were readily identified (Figure 8a and b).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by high-throughput sequencing data in Figure 8A and B

claims.claim: A majority of Saglin haplotypes were mutated only at the target site of gRNA2, suggesting that this gRNA was the most active of the three.
claims.source: Interestingly, a majority of these Saglin haplotypes were mutated only at the target site of gRNA2, suggesting that this gRNA was the most active of the three and that Cas9, confronted to a pool of three Saglin and three Lp gRNAs, will not necessarily cleave all target sites in a given germ cell.
claims.evidence: Inferred from high-throughput sequencing data in Figure 8A and B

claims.claim: Deletions spanning two gRNA target sites were rare in the samples (one instance of such a haplotype was detected, carrying a deletion between gRNA1 and gRNA2).
claims.source: Deletions spanning two gRNA target sites were rare in our samples (one instance of such a haplotype was detected, carrying a deletion between gRNA1 and gRNA2).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by high-throughput sequencing data in Figure 8A and B

claims.claim: At least one haplotype with mutations in all three target sites was recovered after four generations.
claims.source: Inexorably however, Saglin mutants fully refractory to the GD will form in mosquito populations; we recovered at least one haplotype with mutations in all three target sites after four generations (Figure 8a).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by high-throughput sequencing data in Figure 8A

claims.claim: A few GFP negative larvae appeared in populations 2 and 3, amounting to 2.4% of total larvae in generation 14 of population 2.
claims.source: While tracking the frequency of transgenes in [SagGDvasa; Lp::Sc2A10] mosquitoes, we noted the appearance of a few GFP negative larvae in populations 2 and 3. These amounted to 2.4% of total larvae in generation 14 of population 2.
claims.evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of mosquito populations

claims.claim: GFP negative mosquitoes developed to healthy and fertile adults.
claims.source: We COPAS-isolated a sample of these larvae and grew them to adulthood, expecting that they might die during development due to unrescued deleterious mutations in Lp. However, these GFP negative mosquitoes developed to healthy and fertile adults.
claims.evidence: Based on observation of mosquito populations in the laboratory

claims.claim: Sequencing the Lp gene in 12 GFP negative individuals revealed that all were homozygous for the same array of mutations within two of the three Lp gRNA target sequences.
claims.source: Sequencing the Lp gene in 12 individuals revealed that all were homozygous for the same array of mutations within two of the three Lp gRNA target sequences (Figure 8c).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 8C

claims.claim: One mutation deleted three nucleotides before the PAM of gRNA2, removing a single valine from the Lp signal peptide.
claims.source: One mutation deleted three nucleotides before the PAM of gRNA2, removing a single valine from the Lp signal peptide (MWVLGGRRLLWSFLVSLVLIQSVSA, missing valine underlined).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 8C

claims.claim: The other mutation is a 5-base deletion within the target of gRNA3 in the first Lp intron.
claims.source: The other is a 5-base deletion within the target of gRNA3 in the first Lp intron.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 8C

claims.claim: Viability of the homozygous mutant indicates that this combination of mutations, while rendering Lp refractory to Cas9-mediated gene conversion, preserved Lp function.
claims.source: Viability of the homozygous mutant indicates that this combination of mutations, while rendering Lp refractory to Cas9-mediated gene conversion, preserved Lp function.
claims.evidence: Inferred from viability data and sequencing data in Figure 8C

claims.claim: The first of the three gRNA expressed from the gRNA array did not act.
claims.source: This suggested that (i) the first of the three gRNA expressed from the gRNA array did not act; and (ii) combinations of mutations preserving the function of target essential genes can emerge despite the cumulative activity of two gRNAs, which in this case was certainly facilitated by the fact that one of them targeted an intron, more permissive to change.

results.result: The manuscript provides background context on malaria epidemiology and the challenges facing current control strategies. Malaria causes over 245 million cases and 620,000 deaths annually, and while vector control has reduced cases historically, this progress is stalling due to insecticide and drug resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 present established epidemiological facts supported by WHO citation (C1, C2) and general knowledge about vector control trends (C3-C5). These are background claims appropriately cited and consistent with the malaria control literature.

results.result: Lipophorin and Vitellogenin are characterized as the two most abundant secreted proteins in Anopheles hemolymph, with distinct expression patterns: Vitellogenin is induced only after blood feeding and wanes within 3 days, while Lipophorin is expressed constitutively with additional upregulation after blood feeding.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C18-C20 are supported by Coomassie staining data in Figure 1A showing Lp and Vg as major bands, and by citations to Attardo et al., 2005 and Rono et al., 2010 for expression patterns. The experimental evidence and literature support are appropriate.

results.result: The authors engineered the Lipophorin gene to co-express the Sc2A10 single-chain antibody (which binds P. falciparum sporozoites) by inserting Sc2A10 after the Lp signal peptide, utilizing a duplicated furin cleavage site for protein separation, introducing silent mutations to protect against future gRNA targeting, and placing a GFP marker in the first intron.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C21-C25 describe the genetic engineering strategy, which is well-documented in Figure 1B, Materials and Methods, and supported by citation to Zavala et al., 1983 for 2A10 function. The design is logical and the molecular details are clearly presented.

results.result: The Lp::Sc2A10 transgene shows a subtle fitness cost: homozygous mosquitoes are viable and fertile with no obvious fitness defects, but careful analysis over 17 generations revealed transgene frequency decreased by 2.3% per generation, and homozygous females produced fewer progeny than wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by COPAS tracking data in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 2 showing gradual transgene loss, and fertility assays in Supplementary file 3. The fitness cost assessment is appropriately quantified and the conclusion is conservative.

results.result: Mass spectrometry and western blot analysis confirmed that Sc2A10 is expressed and secreted into hemolymph, though at 10-20 fold lower abundance than Lp subunits. Western blots showed proper cleavage of Sc2A10 from ApoLpII, and the chimeric Lp::Sc2A10 protein is expressed at lower levels than wild-type Lp.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are supported by mass spectrometry data in Table 1 showing peptide counts and western blot data in Figure 1D confirming proper cleavage. The quantitative inference about relative abundance (C31) is appropriately calculated from the peptide data corrected for protein size.

results.result: Lp::Sc2A10 transgenic mosquitoes show markedly reduced ability to transmit Plasmodium berghei expressing P. falciparum CSP to mice. Only 29.7% of mice exposed to homozygous transgenic mosquitoes became infected versus 97.1% for controls (p<0.0001). Heterozygous mosquitoes showed comparable transmission blocking (4/12 mice infected vs 17/18 controls, p=0.0006). The effect is PfCSP-specific, as transgenic mosquitoes transmitted control P. berghei normally.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C43 are supported by extensive bite-back experiments shown in Figure 2A-C and Supplementary file 4A-C with appropriate statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test). Sample sizes are adequate (n=34-37 mice for homozygous, n=12-18 for heterozygous), controls are appropriate, and the PfCSP-specificity control (C41-C43) strengthens the conclusion. The statistical significance is properly reported.

results.result: Saglin is characterized as a pro-parasitic gene whose loss reduces parasite prevalence and transmission, is homozygous viable, and has no obvious fitness cost in laboratory conditions, making it an attractive target for gene drive insertion.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C56-C57 are supported by citations to published literature (Okulate et al., 2007; Ghosh et al., 2009; O'Brochta et al., 2019; Klug et al., 2023). These are appropriately cited background claims establishing the rationale for targeting Saglin.

results.result: A suppression gene drive targeting wild-type Lp with zpg-Cas9 and 4 gRNAs was attempted but failed due to Lp haploinsufficiency. Most knock-in events unexpectedly resulted from compound recombination creating a GFP-RFP allele. Heterozygous mosquitoes carrying Lp-GD with either GFP-RFP or Lp::Sc2A10 showed developmental delay and lethality, demonstrating that wild-type Lp is haploinsufficient. Additionally, the zpg promoter showed low activity at the Lp locus.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C55 describe an unsuccessful approach that revealed important biological constraints. The compound recombination (C47) is documented by sequencing and genetic linkage in Figure 3B, haploinsufficiency (C51-C53) is clearly shown in Figure 4B photograph, and low zpg activity (C49, C55) is inferred from inheritance data. The negative result is well-documented and scientifically valuable.

results.result: A Saglin-based gene drive (SagGDzpg) with zpg-Cas9 and 7 gRNAs (3 targeting Saglin, 4 targeting Lp) was constructed and correctly inserted on the X chromosome. However, it showed modest homing rates in G2: 57.7% GFP inheritance at the Lp locus and approximately 54.1% DsRed inheritance at Saglin, only slightly above the 50% expected without homing.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 are supported by experimental design in Figure 5A, genetic crosses showing X-linkage (C59), and COPAS data in Figure 6A quantifying inheritance rates. The modest homing rates are appropriately quantified, though DsRed measurement uncertainty is acknowledged (C63).

results.result: Providing an independent vasa-Cas9 transgene rescued the poor homing of SagGDzpg, resulting in >79% GFP inheritance, demonstrating that the zpg promoter is sensitive to positional effects and has low activity when inserted in Saglin or Lp loci, unlike other reported loci such as DSX or Nudel.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by COPAS data in Figure 6B showing improved homing with vasa-Cas9 complementation. The inference about zpg positional sensitivity (C66) is reasonable given the contrast with published results at other loci (supported by citations to Kyrou et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2021).

results.result: A population of Lp::Sc2A10 combined with SagGDzpg maintained over seven generations showed increased frequency of both alleles (GFP: 59.2%, DsRed: >90%), indicating the modest gene drive was sufficient to counteract the Lp::Sc2A10 fitness cost.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 is supported by COPAS analysis over multiple generations. The data demonstrates that even modest drive activity can overcome fitness costs, though the long-term sustainability is not established.

results.result: An improved Saglin gene drive (SagGDvasa) using vasa-Cas9 instead of zpg-Cas9 was constructed with 6 U6-gRNA units. It correctly inserted on the X chromosome and showed high homing rates in G2: 93% in males (391/405 GFP+) and 90.2% at Lp locus and 61.4% at Saglin locus in females. The vasa promoter was highly active at the Saglin locus, and western blotting confirmed Saglin knockout in homozygous mosquitoes.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C75 are supported by experimental design in Figure 5B, genetic crosses confirming X-linkage (C69), detailed inheritance data in Table 2 and COPAS analysis (C71-C73), and western blot in Figure 5C (C75). The high homing rates represent a major improvement over SagGDzpg and are well-quantified.

results.result: Population dynamics over >30 generations showed that Lp::Sc2A10 rapidly spread in all populations, with most becoming predominantly homozygous. DsRed-only individuals were absent early on, confirming lethality of SagGDvasa without a protected Lp allele. Several populations appeared fixed for Lp::Sc2A10, though population 2 showed reversal after G14. DsRed-negative individuals (up to 30%) persisted in some populations, likely representing drive-resistant Saglin mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C81 are supported by extensive COPAS tracking data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5 across 8 populations over many generations. The reciprocal dependence of the two transgenes is clearly demonstrated, and the emergence of resistance alleles is documented. This is a major result showing the system's behavior over evolutionary time.

results.result: High-throughput sequencing of DsRed-negative larvae from populations 1 and 2 revealed diverse Saglin mutations. While most alleles were still wild-type, various mutations were detected, predominantly at gRNA2 target site, suggesting it was most active. Deletions spanning two gRNA sites were rare, but at least one haplotype with mutations at all three sites was recovered after four generations.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by amplicon sequencing data shown in Figure 8A-B. The analysis appropriately characterizes the spectrum of resistance mutations and their distribution across gRNA target sites. The inference about gRNA2 activity (C84) is reasonable from the mutation patterns.

results.result: GFP-negative larvae appeared in populations 2 and 3 (2.4% at G14 in population 2) and developed into healthy, fertile adults. Sequencing revealed all 12 individuals were homozygous for the same mutations: a 3-nucleotide deletion removing one valine from the Lp signal peptide (gRNA2 site) and a 5-base deletion in the first intron (gRNA3 site). This combination preserved Lp function while conferring resistance to gene conversion, and indicates the first gRNA did not act.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 are supported by COPAS data, viability observations, and sequencing data in Figure 8C. The identification of a functional, drive-resistant Lp allele is a critical finding. However, the sample size is limited (n=12) and all from the same populations, so the generalizability of this specific mutation combination is uncertain. The inference that gRNA1 did not act (C93) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: PCR and sequencing analysis of mosquitoes from generation 32 revealed genetic instability in the gRNA array. Two derivative alleles dominated: one retaining 5 of 6 gRNAs and another retaining only 2 gRNAs. Deletions occurred post-integration (verified by resequencing the original plasmid), likely early in population evolution as the same deletion was found in independently bred populations 1 and 2. The Cas9 gene remained intact despite gRNA deletions.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 are supported by PCR and sequencing data in Figure 9. The genetic instability of repetitive gRNA arrays is well-documented and represents an important limitation of the system. The verification that deletions occurred post-integration (C95) and the timing inference (C96) are appropriately supported.

results.result: [SagGDvasa; Lp::Sc2A10] mosquitoes maintained markedly decreased ability to transmit Plasmodium after >20 generations. In two experiments, 10 of 12 mice exposed to transgenic mosquitoes remained uninfected, compared to 4/4 control mice becoming infected.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by bite-back experiments in Supplementary files 4D-E. However, the sample sizes are small (n=6 and n=6 mice for transgenics, n=4 controls total), and the authors acknowledge they cannot strictly confirm whether Saglin knockout enhanced protection. The result demonstrates persistence of transmission-blocking activity but is limited in statistical power.

results.result: A CRISPR/Cas9-based gene drive was designed and installed in Saglin that disrupts this pro-parasitic gene and cleaves wild-type Lipophorin, causing Lp::Sc2A10 to replace wild-type and hitchhike with the Saglin drive. The drive reached high levels in caged populations and efficiently promoted spread of Lp::Sc2A10, though it generated drive-resistant alleles and showed instability in its gRNA array. This combination is expected to decrease transmission via two mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C17 summarize the overall gene drive strategy and outcomes. The claims are supported by the collective evidence from population dynamics (Figure 7), resistance mutations (Figure 8), and gRNA instability (Figure 9). The dual mechanism expectation (C17) is reasonable inference but not directly demonstrated. The result represents the main finding of the paper.

results.result: Transgenic mosquitoes with Lp::Sc2A10 show a markedly decreased ability to transmit Plasmodium berghei expressing P. falciparum circumsporozoite protein to mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C9 is the high-level summary of the transmission-blocking phenotype, supported by the detailed bite-back experiments in claims C35-C43. This is appropriately supported by Figure 2 data.

results.result: The 2A10 antibody targets the highly repeated and conserved NANP motif on the CSP protein across P. falciparum strains. Complete loss of this epitope is unlikely and would probably cause dramatic parasite fitness loss, as CSP is required in several sporozoite processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are discussion points supported by citations to Coppi et al., 2011 and Balaban et al., 2021. These represent reasonable arguments about the durability of the approach against parasite evolution, though they are speculative regarding future evolutionary outcomes.

results.result: The zpg promoter is sensitive to positional effects and its usability in gene drive constructs may be restricted to a subset of genomic loci, showing low activity at Lp and Saglin loci in contrast to DSX or Nudel loci.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 synthesizes the zpg promoter findings from multiple experiments (claims C55, C66) and is supported by experimental data and citations. This is an important technical finding for future gene drive design.

results.result: The genetic design represents a two-component gene drive where Lp::Sc2A10 has no drive capacity itself but rescues lethality and hitchhikes on SagGDvasa's drive capacity. The two loci are reciprocally dependent: Lp::Sc2A10 depends on SagGD for spread, and SagGD depends on Lp::Sc2A10 as a rescue allele. This can be viewed as a two-locus variation of rescue-type gene drives.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 present the conceptual framework for understanding the system, supported by the population dynamics data showing reciprocal dependence (claims C76-C78). The comparison to rescue-type drives (C106) is appropriately cited to Adolfi et al., 2020 and Champer et al., 2020a.

results.result: A novel P. berghei strain was generated combining strong GFP fluorescence from Δp230p-GFP with P. falciparum CSP substitution from Pb-PfCSP strain.
results.evaluation: Claim C107 describes a methodological development detailed in Materials and Methods. The generation of this parasite strain is appropriately documented and represents an important tool for the transmission experiments.
